newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call up, gilts fall on liquidity fears.
newsitem.headline: Indian call up, gilts fall on liquidity fears.

text.p: Indian call money ended Wednesday higher on fears of liquidity tightening after funds outflows towards a bond issue, dealers said.
They said call money ended in the 4.0-4.5 percent range after opening at Tuesday's closing levels of 0.50-0.75 percent. Stray deals were also struck at 5.0 percent, some dealers said.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sells 25 billion rupees of 10-year bonds issued by 25 state governments on April 30 and dealers said they expected good market response to the issue.
"There will definitely be substantial oversubscription," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "Market expectations are that there will be bids for at least 40 billion rupees."
The dealer said market operators expected the RBI to retain a major part or all of the excess bids received.

"This has led to a fear that liquidity will tighten a bit," he said. "Besides a number of lenders kept off the market today as they were holding back their funds for investing in the state loans. All this pushed call money rates up today."
Dealers however said they expected rates to drop on Friday.
"I think rates will fall..maybe not to sub-one percent levels but ceretainly to around 2.0-3.0 percent on Friday," said a dealer at a foreign bank.
Call money has been below 1.0 percent in the past three weeks.
"Liquidity is still good," said the dealer. "At yesterday's repo auction, the RBI rejected bids for more than 46 billion rupees. This is an indication of how much excess funds are floating around."
Dealers said prices of government securities fell in light trade on Wednesday. Trades were worth around 1.88 billion rupees, down from Tuesday's 4.04 billion, dealers said.
"Basically it was a reaction to higher call money rates and expectations of tightening in liquidity," said a dealer. "But volumes were poor."

The 13.50 percent 1998 government of India stock traded on Wednesday at 103.15 rupees against its last traded 103.27, the 12.50 percent 2004 fell to 99.70 from 99.86 and the 13.05 percent 2007 to 101 rupees from 101.20, dealers said.
The money market is largely inactive on Thursday as banks in India's commercial capital of Bombay and most other centres are closed for local holidays.
